Why work with me

Why businesses choose to work with me for performance marketing

The reasons that come up on almost every call, and what you give up in return by not hiring a larger performance marketing agency.

No learning on your budget

Strategy, account structure and spend decisions stay senior on every account. Execution runs through the team, to that direction. Nobody is being trained at your expense.

You hear the bad news first

If something stops working you will hear it from me before you find it in a dashboard. The report leads with what went wrong, because that is the part that needs a decision.

Strategy that starts from the P&L

The question is what a customer can cost and still leave a margin, not what the platform is willing to report. Campaigns are built backwards from that number.

You find out early

Most of the money lost on a new marketer is spent discovering they were wrong. Accounts are structured so the first honest read arrives in weeks rather than quarters.

Fewer clients, by design

Capacity is the constraint and it is chosen. Taking fewer accounts is the only way the senior attention you are paying for actually reaches your account.

You keep everything

Accounts, pixels, data and creative sit in your name from the first day. If this ends you leave with the entire history, which is the part that makes the next thing work.

How I think

The dashboard looks healthy.The business is not.

All five have been described to me on a first call, almost word for word. The symptom is common. The diagnosis usually is not. Most performance marketing agencies treat the symptom, because the symptom is what the brief describes, which is why so many of them end up being solved with more budget.

Two last-click models is not attribution, it is double counting.

Each platform reports every conversion it touched. Add the two together and they describe more revenue than the business actually made. That overlap is not a rounding error. It is the share of your budget whose contribution nobody has ever tested.

What I doMeasure against total revenue, then hold a channel out and watch what really moves.

Average ROAS held. Marginal ROAS had already collapsed.

Your first lakh buys the cheapest impressions available. The fifth buys whatever is left. Blended ROAS keeps looking healthy because it averages the good spend with the bad, which is why the algorithm usually gets blamed instead.

What I doPrice the next rupee, not the whole account. Scale stops where marginal return meets your margin.

ROAS is weighted by revenue. Your P&L is weighted by margin.

Discount-led products convert easily and report beautifully. After cost of goods, shipping, payment fees and returns, the campaign with the strongest ROAS can be the one you are paying to keep running.

What I doSend margin back into the account so the platform bids for profit instead of revenue.

You optimised towards a form, so the platform went and found form fillers.

A platform will get very good at whatever you send back to it. If the only event it sees is a form submission, it will learn to find people who submit forms. Nobody in the account knows which of those a salesperson could ever close.

What I doFeed qualified and closed-won back in, so bidding happens against outcomes sales would recognise.

Blended CAC is a mix, and the mix is flattering you.

Returning customers are cheap to reach and many were coming back anyway. Average them in and acquisition looks affordable. Separate them and you find what a genuinely new customer costs, which is the number that decides whether you can scale at all.

What I doReport new-customer CAC against contribution, and keep retention spend on its own line.

Most of it is not buying media. It is making sure the account is being judged on the right number. That means getting the conversion tracking to agree with what the business actually banked, working out which products or lead types are worth paying for, and then deciding where the next rupee of budget goes. The campaign work follows from that. A performance marketing specialist who is only managing bids and creative is doing the part that matters least.

A specialist, with a team. I read the numbers, set the account structure and make the spend decisions, and that part is not passed to anyone junior. The build work runs through a team of more than ten across paid media, creative, measurement, landing pages and search. You are not choosing between one person's attention and a team's capacity.

Probably nothing in the campaigns for the first fortnight. I would start by checking whether a conversion in Google or Meta matches an order in your backend, because in most accounts it does not. Then work out contribution by product or by lead type, so it is clear which conversions are worth paying for. Then look at what the last slice of spend is earning rather than what the account earns on average. Most reporting shows the average. The marginal number is the one that tells you whether you can scale.

Usually because the platforms are each claiming the same sale, the attribution window is long enough to take credit for people who would have bought anyway, and ROAS is measured on revenue rather than what is left after cost of goods, shipping, payment fees, discounts and returns. A 4x ROAS on a 30 per cent gross margin loses money. In lead generation it shows up as a steady cost per lead while the cost per qualified lead climbs, because the cheap leads are the ones that never answer the phone. The fix is to agree one number with your finance side and judge every campaign against it.

Commonly the account has run out of its best audience and the extra spend is reaching people who were never going to buy. It can also be budget sitting in campaigns that look efficient because they are harvesting demand you already created, creative that has stopped producing winners so frequency rises instead of reach, or a landing page and offer that cannot carry colder traffic. Working out which one it is takes an afternoon in the account.

I do. The strategy, the account structure and the spend decisions are mine, and they stay mine for as long as you are a client. The build work, creative production, landing pages and reporting run through my team, to that direction. You are not handed to someone junior after the first month.

Usually not in execution, which is the part in-house teams tend to do well. It is measurement, because building attribution your finance side will sign off on is a specialist job nobody in-house has time for, and the decision about where the next rupee goes across Google, Meta and LinkedIn rather than optimising each channel on its own. If your team is capable and mainly needs direction, that is a smaller engagement and I will say so.

Edit access to the ad accounts, analytics and wherever orders or leads land, plus your cost of goods or your cost per qualified lead. The first week is the audit and the measurement work. Structural changes usually go live in week two. Anything that depends on learning, such as creative testing or a bidding change, needs a full buying cycle before it can be judged, which for most businesses is six to twelve weeks.

That is your choice, not a fixed rule. A flat monthly retainer suits a stable scope. A fee based on effort suits work that changes shape month to month. A percentage of ad spend suits an account where media buying is the main lever. Revenue share works where both sides can see the economics clearly enough for it to be fair. Audits are fixed scope with a written output and no obligation to continue, and most engagements start there, because neither side can price ongoing work honestly before seeing the account.

Ask about pricing on WhatsApp

Only on the percentage of ad spend model, where that is the arrangement. On a retainer or an effort based fee it does not. The fee moves when the scope moves, not when the budget does. Revenue share tracks what the spend produces rather than the spend itself.

Then I tell you, with the number that says so, and we stop. Sometimes the honest answer is that paid is not the constraint, and the problem is margin, pricing, product or the offer. I would rather say that in month two than bill you for a year while the account treads water.

Everything stays with you. The ad accounts, the conversion tracking, the landing pages, the audiences, the reporting and the documentation live in your own accounts and remain yours. Nothing has to be handed back, rebuilt or bought out, and whoever picks it up next can see what was done and why.

Yes. The accounts I run include businesses selling into the United States, the United Kingdom, the UAE and Australia. What matters more than time zone is whether the measurement is sound, and whether someone on your side can make a decision in the week the numbers say to.
